---
title: "Get started in Python"
---

DenMark measures how gene expression depends on local cell density in
single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomics data. Cell locations form a
point pattern and the counts of a gene are its marks. After the cells are
binned on a regular grid over the tissue, the DenMark model for grid cell $g$
with area $|g|$ inside the tissue, cell count $Y(g)$ and summed expression
$M(g)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y(g) &\sim \text{Poisson}\{\lambda_1(g)\}, & \log\lambda_1(g) &= \log|g| + \beta_0 + a_{11}w_1(g),\\
M(g)\mid Y(g) &\sim \text{Poisson}\{\lambda_2(g)\}, & \log\lambda_2(g) &= \beta_1 + \log\{Y(g)+0.05\} + a_{21}w_1(g) + a_{22}w_2(g),
\end{aligned}
$$

where $w_1$ and $w_2$ are independent unit-variance Gaussian processes with
Matern-3/2 covariance, approximated by Hilbert space basis functions (HSGP).
With $a_{11} = \sigma_1$, $a_{21} = \sigma_2\rho$ and
$a_{22} = \sigma_2\sqrt{1-\rho^2}$, the parameter $\rho$ (`Astar[2,1]` in
Stan) is the density-expression correlation.

This page runs the workflow on the bundled toy data, where the true
correlations are known, so every estimate can be checked against the truth.
The Python package `denmark` builds the same Stan data as the R package and
fits the same Stan models through [cmdstanpy](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanpy/);
[Get started in R](DenMark.html) walks through the same steps in R, and
[R and Python side by side](r-python.html) lists the function names of both. The
code below is shown without its output, and the package tests run it as written.

## Installation

DenMark fits its models with Stan through cmdstanpy, which needs a working
CmdStan installation, and computes the tissue boundary with shapely. Install
them once:

```bash
pip install "denmark[boundary,plot] @ git+https://github.com/StaGill/DenMark#subdirectory=python"
python -m cmdstanpy.install_cmdstan
```

`denmark` needs Python 3.9 or later. The extra `boundary` adds shapely (2.0 or
later) for the tissue boundary and `plot` adds matplotlib for the figures.
`install_cmdstan` downloads and builds CmdStan once per machine and needs a
C++ toolchain.

## The toy data

`dm.datasets.load_toy()` returns a tissue section simulated by
`denmark_simulate()` in R: 7,449 cells in an irregular, lobed section inside a
6 x 4 window, one row per cell, with the cell type and the counts of three
genes. The 3,449 Tumor cells are the population analyzed; their true
density-expression correlations are 0.6 for geneA, 0 for geneB and -0.6 for
geneC. The 4,000 Other cells only delineate the tissue.

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import denmark as dm

toy = dm.datasets.load_toy()
print(toy.head())
print(toy["celltype"].value_counts())
tumor = toy[toy["celltype"] == "Tumor"].drop(columns="celltype")
truth = {"geneA": 0.6, "geneB": 0.0, "geneC": -0.6}
```

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
points = ax.scatter(tumor["x"], tumor["y"], c=tumor["geneA"], s=2, cmap="magma")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
fig.colorbar(points, ax=ax, label="geneA")
```

## Tissue boundary

A tissue section is rarely a rectangle. If the grid covered the bounding box
of the cells, grid cells outside the tissue would hold no cells because there
is no tissue there, and the model would read them as regions of low cell
density. `dm.alpha_shape()` delineates the tissue as an alpha shape: it
triangulates the cell locations and keeps every Delaunay triangle whose
circumradius is below $\alpha$, by default three times the median Delaunay
edge length. The boundary is computed from all cells of the section, not only
the Tumor cells, because the region where a Tumor cell could have been
observed is the whole tissue. The result holds the polygon (`.polygon`), the
alpha (`.alpha`) and the tissue area (`.area`).

```python
tissue = dm.alpha_shape(toy["x"], toy["y"])
print(tissue.alpha, tissue.area)
```

## Gridding

`dm.buildgridpp()` assigns every cell to one grid cell and returns the cell
counts $Y(g)$ and the summed expression $M(g)$. Grid cells are ordered with
x varying fastest. With `boundary`, the grid spans the extent of the tissue,
and each grid cell is classified as interior (entirely inside the tissue),
boundary (partly inside) or exterior, with its area inside the tissue in the
column `area`.

```python
gridded = dm.buildgridpp(10, tumor, gene="geneA", boundary=tissue)
print(gridded["grid"].head())
print(gridded["grid"]["type"].value_counts())
fig = dm.plot_boundary(toy, tissue, grid=gridded, highlight=toy["celltype"] == "Tumor")
```

Exterior grid cells are dropped from the model, and boundary grid cells enter
with their area inside the tissue, so the area offset $\log|g|$ differs
between grid cells. `dm.plot_grid()` shows the gridded counts inside the
tissue.

```python
fig = dm.plot_grid(gridded)
```

`dm.prepare_data()` builds the Stan input that `dm.DenMark()` uses: it drops
the exterior grid cells, centers the region of interest at the origin, uses
the grid centroids as HSGP coordinates and sets the HSGP domain to
`boundfactor` times the half-ranges. With a boundary, `log_grid_area` holds one
value per grid cell in the model.

```python
prep = dm.prepare_data(tumor, gene="geneA", grid_size=10, basis=10, boundfactor=1.5,
                       boundary=tissue)
stan_data = prep["stan_data"]
print({k: stan_data[k] for k in ("n", "mstar", "L", "mrange")})
print(stan_data["log_grid_area"][:5])
```

## Fitting the model

`dm.DenMark()` grids the data, compiles the Stan model on first use and
samples; the compiled model is cached in a user directory (set by the
environment variable `DENMARK_CACHE_DIR`, by default `~/.cache/denmark`), so
later sessions reuse it. With `boundary`, it fits the variable-area model
`DenMark-vararea.stan`, the same model with one area offset per grid cell;
without it, the bounding box of the cells is gridded with a common grid area.
The settings below keep the page fast; for real data, use the defaults (four
chains of 1,000 warm-up and 1,000 sampling iterations and `basis=25`) and check
the diagnostics.

```python
fit = dm.DenMark(tumor, gene="geneA", boundary=tissue, grid_size=10, basis=10,
                 boundfactor=1.5, chains=2, iter_warmup=500, iter_sampling=500,
                 seed=2024, quiet=True)
print(fit)
```

## Posterior summaries

`fit.summary()` reports the intercepts, the length-scales `ell[1]` and
`ell[2]`, $\rho$ and the field standard deviations, with R-hat and effective
sample sizes.

```python
print(fit.summary()[["variable", "mean", "sd", "q2.5", "q97.5", "rhat", "ess_bulk"]])
```

`fit.draws()` returns one row per posterior draw, including $\rho$. The red
line marks the true value.

```python
draws = fit.draws()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
ax.hist(draws["rho"], bins=40, density=True, color="0.8")
ax.axvline(0, linestyle="--", color="0.3")
ax.axvline(truth["geneA"], color="#B2182B")
ax.set_xlim(-1, 1)
ax.set_xlabel("rho")
ax.set_ylabel("Posterior density")
```

## Latent fields

`fit.fields()` decomposes, for every grid cell in the model, the log cell
intensity $\beta_0 + a_{11}w_1$ and the log expression per cell
$\beta_1 + a_{21}w_1 + a_{22}w_2$ into the density field $a_{11}w_1$, the
density-shared part of expression $a_{21}w_1$ and the expression-specific
part $a_{22}w_2$.

```python
fields = fit.fields()
print(fields[["grid_index", "Y", "M", "eta1", "a11w1", "eta2", "a21w1", "a22w2"]].head())
fig = dm.plot_fields(fit, fields=fields)
```

## Spatial correlation ranges

`fit.decay()` gives the posterior spatial correlation of the density and
expression fields as a function of distance, and the practical range, the
distance at which the correlation falls to 0.05.

```python
decay = fit.decay()
print(decay["ranges"])
fig = dm.plot_decay(fit, decay=decay)
```

## Scanning genes for density-correlated genes

`dm.scan_genes()` fits DenMark to each gene and calls it a positively (PCG)
or negatively (NCG) density-correlated gene when the 95% credible interval
of $\rho$ lies above or below 0, and not a DCG otherwise.

```python
scan = dm.scan_genes(tumor, genes=["geneA", "geneB", "geneC"], boundary=tissue,
                     grid_size=10, basis=10, boundfactor=1.5, chains=2,
                     iter_warmup=500, iter_sampling=500, seed=2024, verbose=False)
print(scan[["gene", "rho_mean", "rho_lower", "rho_upper", "class", "max_rhat"]])
fig = dm.plot_scan(scan)
```

## Checking the estimates against the truth

With true values of 0.6, 0 and -0.6, the expected calls are PCG for geneA,
not DCG for geneB and NCG for geneC. The table compares each posterior mean
and 95% credible interval with the true $\rho$; `covered` shows whether the
interval contains it.

```python
check = pd.DataFrame({"gene": scan["gene"], "truth": scan["gene"].map(truth),
                      "estimate": scan["rho_mean"], "lower": scan["rho_lower"],
                      "upper": scan["rho_upper"], "class": scan["class"]})
check["covered"] = (check["lower"] <= check["truth"]) & (check["truth"] <= check["upper"])
print(check)
```

## Using your own data

DenMark needs one row per cell with the coordinates in columns `x` and `y`
and raw counts in one column per gene. Compute the tissue boundary from all
cells of the section, then analyze the cells of one population: filter
uninformative genes, fit one gene, then scan the panel; with `save_dir`, each
gene is saved as it finishes and an interrupted scan resumes where it
stopped.

```python
cells = pd.read_csv("cells.csv")   # all cells: x, y, celltype and gene counts
tissue = dm.alpha_shape(cells["x"], cells["y"])
focal = cells[cells["celltype"] == "Tumor"].drop(columns="celltype")
genes = dm.filter_genes(focal.drop(columns=["x", "y"]))
fit = dm.DenMark(focal[["x", "y", genes[0]]], gene=genes[0], boundary=tissue,
                 grid_size=15, basis=25, boundfactor=1.5)
dcg = dm.scan_genes(focal[["x", "y"] + genes], boundary=tissue, grid_size=15, basis=25,
                    save_dir="denmark_scan")
```

`fit.check_hsgp()` compares the posterior length-scales with a rule of thumb
for the number of basis functions and the boundary factor, and
`dm.save_result()` keeps a fit for later sessions.
